docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction
docs.text: Chapter 1

docs.title: The Rationale of Parameter-Free Ground Classification of ALS, ULS, and TLS Point Clouds
docs.text: FAST-GC (Fully Adaptive Self-Tuning Ground Classification) is a parameter-free algorithm for classifying LiDAR ground points from non-ground points in fully automated way and reconstructing terrain surfaces from airborne laser scanning (ALS), UAV laser scanning (ULS), and terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) observations. The algorithm adapts terrain-support estimation internally to the acquisition geometry, sampling characteristics, and local terrain conditions, thereby reducing dependence on scene-specific parameter calibration. This chapter presents the principal classification and terrain-reconstruction evidence, followed by a concise operational introduction.

docs.title: 1.1 Why ground classification matters
docs.text: Ground-point classification is a fundamental stage in LiDAR data processing because omission of legitimate ground returns and inclusion of non-ground observations propagate into digital elevation models (DEMs), height normalization, canopy-height models, and subsequent geospatial products. The classification challenge varies with terrain gradient, canopy cover, ground-return availability, and sensor acquisition geometry. FAST-GC addresses these variations through internally adaptive processing rather than requiring users to recalibrate classification settings for each scene. The method remains algorithmically parameterized; its self-tuning character refers specifically to the absence of scene-specific manual parameter calibration in the evaluated workflows.

docs.title: 1.2 Preserving terrain morphology: comparison with established filters
docs.text:
The controlled comparison used ALS observations from the southern Sierra Nevada Mountains, California, originally compiled by Jin et al. (2020). The source dataset contains twenty 500 × 500 m sites spanning contrasting forest cover and topographic conditions. For the controlled evaluation, the selected source blocks were renumbered; comparison Sites 2–5 correspond to original Jin et al. blocks 1, 12, 13, and 15, respectively. Figure 1.1 compares 0.5 m DEMs generated from FAST-GC, Cloth Simulation Filtering (CSF), Progressive TIN Densification (PTD), and Progressive Morphological Filtering (PMF). Although all four algorithms recover the broad terrain gradient, their ability to preserve local terrain morphology diverges as topographic complexity increases. Spatially contiguous elevation discrepancies are more extensive for the conventional filters in the more demanding terrain scenes.

Figure 1.1. Comparison of 0.5 m digital elevation models derived from FAST-GC, CSF, PTD, and PMF across selected southern Sierra Nevada ALS benchmark sites (Jin et al., 2020; comparison Sites 2–5, original blocks 1, 12, 13, and 15). Elevations are normalized relative to the minimum terrain elevation within each site. Red polygon boundaries identify spatially contiguous areas where the absolute difference from the reference DEM derived from original ground-classified returns (class 2) is at least 0.25 m. Rows represent sites and columns represent classification methods.

docs.title: 1.3 Robustness across steep slopes and reduced point density
docs.text:
Terrain reconstruction errors exhibit a pronounced dependence on reference terrain slope (Figure 1.2). Cell-level DEM residuals from the same Sierra Nevada benchmark were pooled within 10° slope intervals to evaluate mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE). Differences among algorithms remained comparatively limited under gentle terrain conditions but increased substantially toward steeper slopes. At 70–80°, FAST-GC achieved a DEM MAE of 1.00 m, compared with 3.12–12.75 m for the evaluated conventional filters. These results demonstrate greater preservation of complex terrain within the controlled benchmark, rather than invariant accuracy across all landscapes.

Figure 1.2. Slope-dependent terrain reconstruction errors for FAST-GC, CSF, PTD, and PMF using the Jin et al. (2020) southern Sierra Nevada ALS benchmark (comparison Sites 2–5). Cell-level residuals between method-derived and reference 0.5 m DEMs are grouped into 10° reference-slope classes and summarized as (a) mean absolute error and (b) root mean square error. Increasing errors with slope indicate progressive loss of terrain-reconstruction accuracy.

The availability of terrain-supporting observations also changes with LiDAR sampling density. Figure 1.3 illustrates ground and non-ground separation along the same representative ALS terrain profile after deterministic thinning to approximately 4 and 6 points/m². Ground classification remains visually coherent beneath vegetation and across varying terrain conditions. In the wider twenty-site Sierra Nevada assessment, a reduction in median point density from 9.84 to 3.84 points/m² maintained F1-score near 0.97 and intersection-over-union near 0.95, while DEM MAE increased from 0.07 to 0.11 m. These findings indicate that reduced sampling support need not translate directly into a proportional loss of classification agreement, although terrain-surface error remains sensitive to the available ground observations.

Figure 1.3. FAST-GC ground classification under reduced ALS point densities using the Jin et al. (2020) southern Sierra Nevada benchmark. The same representative terrain profile is shown after deterministic thinning to (a) D4 (approximately 4 points/m²) and (b) D6 (approximately 6 points/m²). Red points indicate classified ground returns and green points indicate non-ground vegetation returns. Circled locations and enlarged insets illustrate ground–non-ground separation under contrasting local terrain and canopy conditions.

docs.title: 1.4 Cross-platform consistency: ALS, ULS, and TLS
docs.text:
Cross-platform consistency was evaluated using the central European forest LiDAR dataset of Weiser et al. (2022), specifically plot BR01 in Bretten, Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The independently acquired ALS, TLS, and ULS observations differ in sampling geometry, point density, acquisition date, and canopy condition. Accordingly, correspondence was assessed at the terrain-surface level rather than by direct point-wise comparison. FAST-GC ground returns were used to reconstruct independent 0.5 m DEMs, and spatially coincident cells were compared across six platform and canopy-condition combinations (Figure 1.4). Across the common footprints, the DEMs exhibited R² and concordance correlation coefficients of at least 0.99, with RMSE of 0.10–0.16 m. The ULS-based comparisons covered 5.47 ha, whereas comparisons involving TLS were restricted to 0.48 ha. The results indicate strong terrain-surface correspondence despite substantial differences in the underlying LiDAR observations.

Figure 1.4. Cross-platform correspondence of independently reconstructed 0.5 m DEMs at forest plot BR01, Bretten, Germany, from the multi-platform dataset of Weiser et al. (2022). Panels compare (a) ULS leaf-off versus leaf-on, (b) ALS versus ULS leaf-off, (c) ALS versus ULS leaf-on, (d) ALS versus TLS, (e) TLS versus ULS leaf-off, and (f) TLS versus ULS leaf-on. Hexagonal bins represent paired DEM-cell elevations; dashed red lines indicate 1:1 correspondence and blue lines indicate fitted regressions. Comparisons use overlapping footprints of 5.47 ha for ULS-based pairs and 0.48 ha for pairs involving TLS. The results characterize terrain-surface agreement, not point-wise classification accuracy.

docs.title: 1.5 Install FAST-GC
docs.text:
Book versus software

The FAST-GC Book is documentation only. You do not need to install the book to process LiDAR data. The commands below install and run the separate FAST-GC package.

The FAST-GC v0.2.1 release documentation lists support for Python 3.12–3.14. Check the package's current release requirements before installing a later version.

docs.title: Recommended installation
docs.text:
In a terminal with an appropriate Python installation:

python -m pip install fastgc

Verify that the command-line application is available:

fastgc --version
fastgc --help

If you intend to develop FAST-GC itself, consult the package repository's installation guidance rather than the documentation-book setup.

docs.title: 1.6 Prepare your first LiDAR file
docs.text:
For the introductory workflow, use an existing .las or .laz point cloud and note its acquisition platform. Place the file in a working directory, or supply its full path.

The following example assumes an ALS file named input.laz. Replace that filename and sensor mode with the values appropriate to your data.

Input data

Start with a small, representative file so that you can inspect the classification visually before running a larger batch.

docs.title: 1.7 Run your first ground classification
docs.text:
The FAST-GC release README documents this basic command:

fastgc --in_path "input.laz" --sensor_mode ALS --products FAST_GC

To specify a destination directory explicitly:

fastgc --in_path "input.laz" --out_dir "FASTGC_output" --sensor_mode ALS --products FAST_GC
Argument Purpose --in_path Path to the input point cloud --sensor_mode Acquisition mode: ALS, ULS, or TLS --products FAST_GC Request the ground-classification product --out_dir Specify an output directory

These examples show the documented interface, not an execution performed for this book. File naming and the complete output directory layout should be confirmed from a real run before adding an output-tree example.

docs.title: 1.8 Closing perspective
docs.text:
The comparative assessments demonstrate that ground-point classification performance is governed not only by point-wise classification agreement but also by the capacity to preserve terrain morphology under increasing topographic complexity, reduced sampling support, and contrasting acquisition geometries. Across the evaluated datasets, FAST-GC maintained comparatively stable classification and terrain-reconstruction performance without scene-specific parameter calibration. The cross-platform analysis further demonstrated close correspondence among independently reconstructed ALS, ULS, and TLS terrain surfaces. These findings establish the practical relevance of sensor-adaptive ground classification for heterogeneous LiDAR observations, while recognizing that reconstruction uncertainty remains dependent on terrain and ground-return availability. Algorithmic details and additional evaluations are addressed in Chapter 3.

Dataset references and advanced reading. The southern Sierra Nevada ALS benchmark is from Jin et al. (2020); the multi-platform German forest observations are from Weiser et al. (2022). For full dataset citations, experimental protocols, and methodological details, see Fareed, N., Numata, I., Silva, C. A., & Prichard, S. J. (2026), FAST-GC: A Fully Adaptive Self-Tuning Ground Classification Algorithm for Multi-Platform LiDAR Sensors, research preprint (not peer-reviewed).

docs.title: Chapter 3 — FAST-GIS: LiDAR survey sampling, plot extraction, and downstream products
docs.text: Software scope: FAST-GC 0.2.1, fastgc gis and fastgc --workflow plots-run. Demonstration: BR01 Airborne Laser Scanning (ALS) survey, five randomly selected circular plots, Plot 005 visual examples. Reproducibility status: the five-plot unbuffered clipping run and its downstream raster-mask failure were observed in terminal logs. A buffered Plot 005 clipping metadata file supplied with the figures was independently inspected: point_extent=core_plus_buffer, buffer_m=5, core_points=79,211, points_written=162,139. The uploaded rasters demonstrate downstream product existence; a complete successful terminal log for all five buffered plots was not supplied. The two standalone elevation/height GeoTIFF labels remain provisional.

docs.title: 3.1 Scope and scientific motivation
docs.text:
FAST-GIS bridges a georeferenced LiDAR survey and repeatable plot-level analysis. It discovers survey files, resolves survey geometry and coordinate reference systems (Coordinate Reference System (CRS)), selects or imports plot footprints, clips LAS/LAZ points, publishes a machine-readable collection, and hands that collection to FAST-GC for ground classification and forest/terrain products. Plot core and processing buffer are distinct: processing uses extra spatial context, while mapped raster results are masked back to the core polygon.

FAST-GIS is not a ground classifier or canopy-height estimator. Those operations are performed by downstream FAST-GC workflows. This distinction is important for provenance, especially when rough-height sampling is used before ground classification.

docs.text:

For the random path, the integrated CLI passes shape and radius, but not the separate width_m, height_m, or rotation_deg options to the random sampler; those dimension controls are principally relevant to continuous layouts. Do not assume identical parameter behavior across modes.

docs.title: The running case study: follow Plot 005 from source to measurements
docs.text:
This chapter uses one consistent observational example: Plot 005, selected as one of five random circular cores from the BR01 ALS survey. All point-cloud and raster panels below refer to this same Plot 005, unless explicitly labeled schematic. Readers can therefore compare canopy features, terrain patterns, point support, and vertical structure without switching study sites. The diagrams illustrating other shapes and sampling strategies are conceptual drawings, not additional BR01 observations.

Stage Same Plot 005 input/output What to inspect in the figure Scientific question 1. Survey and clipping BR01 source → Plot_005.laz + Clip_Plot_005.json Circular core vs buffered neighborhood Which points belong to the measurement area? 2. Ground classification FAST_GC Ground/non-ground colors in plan and profile Where is the terrain under the trees? 3. Height normalization FAST_NORMALIZED Height above ground in profile How tall and vertically layered is vegetation? 4. Surface and terrain Digital Elevation Model (DEM)/DSM/CHM and FAST_TERRAIN Height surface vs slope, aspect, roughness How do topography and canopy differ? 5. Canopy and structure FAST_STRUCTURE Cover, height, diversity and vertical gaps How complex is the forest within the plot? 6. Geometric descriptors Structure geometry rasters Linearity, planarity, anisotropy What 3D arrangements are represented?

Figure-reading convention: Maps are north-up georeferenced views. Side views use elevation or normalized height as labeled. A raster cell's color represents the metric and units on that panel's own colorbar, not a common scale across products. White/no-data cells are not automatically zero vegetation. Each figure appears once in its relevant section. Where the MkDocs GLightbox plugin is enabled, clicking the image opens the original PNG for zooming.

docs.title: 3.2 Plot geometry and processing footprint
docs.text:
The plot core is the intended measurement area. A processing buffer of width surrounds it; its points provide neighborhood context for classification and raster interpolation.

Geometry Definition / formula What it measures Typical use Circle Circular area specified by centre and radius Fixed-radius area Inventory plots, local forest structure Square Four equal sides and right angles Equal-sided area Grid-compatible sampling Rectangle Four sides with specified width and height Elongated survey area Transects and edge studies Ellipse Oval specified by major and minor dimensions Directional oval area Elongated features Regular hexagon Six equal sides Compact six-sided area Spatially regular tessellation

For a circular core with a 15 m radius, the nominal area is 706.86 square metres. A 5 m buffer expands the processing radius to 20 m and the nominal processing area to 1,256.64 square metres. These are geometric areas, not guarantees of observed point coverage.

Boundary interpretation: Point clouds used during processing can extend beyond the 15 m core. Core-masked raster products should not be mistaken for rectangular full-extent outputs or for a 20 m measurement plot.

Figure 3.A. Schematic plot geometries (not survey-derived measurements): circle, square, rectangle, ellipse, and regular hexagon. The centre dot denotes the plot reference point.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Processing core and buffer
docs.text: Figure 3.B. Measurement core (15 m radius) and 5 m processing buffer; conceptual diagram, not to scale with any survey map. The buffer supports computations; the core defines the reported plot.

Random sampling selects eligible locations reproducibly; continuous sampling follows a lattice; rough-height sampling balances plots across height strata; imported sampling honors externally supplied boundaries. Shapes and positions are illustrative, not actual BR01 plot coordinates.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Random sampling: complete BR01 example
docs.text:
Random sampling uses an observed-coverage grid to identify eligible centres, avoids overlaps between processing footprints, and uses a seed for reproducibility. The selected centres are therefore constrained by survey coverage rather than uniformly sampled from every coordinate inside the survey bounding box.

conda activate fastgc

fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_Buffered_Test" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --sampling random `
    --plots 5 `
    --shape circle `
    --radius 15 `
    --buffer 5 `
    --seed 42
Parameter Function / definition Configuration guidance --in_path Source LAS/LAZ file or survey directory Use georeferenced source data; here BR01 ALS --out_dir New published FAST-GIS workspace Choose a new directory; the sampler publishes transactionally --sensor_mode Sensor type ALS, Uncrewed Aerial Laser Scanning (ULS), or Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS); here ALS --sampling Selection strategy random, continuous, imported, rough_height_stratified --plots Requested plot count Here 5; default 30; placement may fail if coverage is insufficient --shape Core polygon geometry Here circle; defaults to hexagon --radius Core radius, metres Here 15 m; default 15 m --buffer Extra processing support, metres Here 5 m; default 5 m; recommended for this core-masking example --seed Random-number seed Here 42; default 42 --coverage_cell_m XY occupancy-cell size Default 5 m; smaller cells can improve footprint screening at additional cost --chunk_size LAS points read per chunk Default 500,000; adjust for available memory

Observed evidence: A five-plot, zero-buffer run completed clipping in 9.76 s for the 12,531,758-point BR01 input, but subsequent plots-run stopped at raster masking. The uploaded buffered Plot 005 metadata establishes that the 5 m buffer configuration creates the expected core_plus_buffer contract. Do not present the 9.76 s timing as a benchmark for the buffered run.

docs.title: 3.4 Continuous/systematic plot sampling
docs.text:
The continuous sampler searches a spatial lattice of candidate plot centres and evaluates layout against observed XY coverage. --overlap_m specifies intended overlap between adjacent core footprints; --phase_steps controls lattice-offset search. Its purpose is regular spatial coverage, not a statistically independent random sample.

fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_Continuous" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --sampling continuous `
    --shape square `
    --width_m 30 `
    --height_m 30 `
    --overlap_m 5 `
    --buffer 5 `
    --phase_steps 10
Parameter Function / definition Configuration guidance --sampling continuous Systematic layout selection Use for spatially distributed, regular plot coverage --shape square Plot footprint Circle, hexagon, square, rectangle, ellipse supported by geometry module --width_m Core width Default 30 m; controls square/rectangle/ellipse geometry --height_m Core height Default 30 m; used for rectangle/ellipse; square enforces equal sides --overlap_m Core-footprint overlap Default 5 m; must be nonnegative --buffer Additional processing context Default 5 m --phase_steps Candidate lattice phases Default 10; higher values can increase layout-search work --rotation_deg Footprint rotation Default 0°; relevant for supported continuous layouts --coverage_cell_m Observed occupancy grid resolution Default 5 m; trade-off between detail and cost

Validation: This is a source-supported CLI example, not a run demonstrated by the uploaded BR01 outputs. It should be tested before attaching measured timing or plot-count claims.

docs.title: 3.5 Rough-height-stratified circular sampling
docs.text: This mode samples low-, medium-, and high-rough-height plots before ground classification. It requires an existing DSM and a single LAS/LAZ source. The rough-height proxy subtracts a local low-return elevation estimate from the digital surface model and sets negative results to zero. This proxy is not a validated canopy-height model. The sampler classifies each candidate plot by the median valid rough-height value inside its circular core, and allocates an equal number of plots to three strata. The requested plot count must therefore be divisible by three.

docs.title: Step A — Create the required DSM
docs.text:
fastgc `
    --workflow run `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_DSM" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --products FAST_DSM `
    --grid_res 1.0

docs.text:
fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_RoughHeight" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --sampling rough_height_stratified `
    --dsm_path "G:\FASTGC_BR01_DSM\FAST_DSM\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.tif" `
    --plots 9 `
    --shape circle `
    --radius 15 `
    --buffer 5 `
    --low_max 5 `
    --medium_max 15 `
    --seed 42
Parameter Function / definition Configuration guidance --dsm_path Existing DSM GeoTIFF Required; DSM and LAS must have matching embedded projected CRS --plots Total stratified sample Positive multiple of 3; here 9 --shape circle Stratified core geometry Only circle supported by this mode --low_max Low/medium threshold in rough-height metres Default 5 m; adjust for vegetation height distribution --medium_max Medium/high threshold Default 15 m; must exceed low_max --radius, --buffer Core radius and processing support Defaults 15 m and 5 m --seed Reproducible candidate ordering Default 42

Known limitation from the earlier BR01 attempt: LAS CRS WKT and DSM EPSG:25832 were not considered equal by the sampler's strict CRS comparison, even though both described ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N. The command above is illustrative, not validated on this specific input/DSM pair. Do not silently alter CRS metadata or describe a failed attempt as a successful demonstration.

docs.title: 3.6 Imported plot definitions
docs.text:
FAST-GIS accepts pre-existing plot polygons or centres from KML, KMZ, shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, and CSV. Vector coordinates must be interpretable in a known CRS; CSV centres may need --source_crs.

fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_Imported" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --sampling imported `
    --plot_file "G:\Survey\BR01_plots.geojson" `
    --buffer 5
Parameter Function / definition Configuration guidance --sampling imported Use externally defined plot geometries No random selection; footprints come from plot file --plot_file Input plot-definition file KML/KMZ/SHP/GPKG/GeoJSON/CSV; example path must exist --layer Layer selector Supply for a multilayer GeoPackage when necessary --source_crs CRS override For missing LAS/LAZ CRS or CSV plot centres --buffer Processing margin Default 5 m; preserve core polygon in metadata

Important: G:\Survey\BR01_plots.geojson is a placeholder for a real user-supplied plot file, not an observed artifact from this case study.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Using the author's own field-plot boundaries
docs.text:
An investigator who already has mapped inventory plots does not need to generate random or continuous plots. The imported mode clips the LiDAR survey using the provided geometries. Supported inputs from the supplied FAST-GIS modules include ESRI Shapefile (.shp plus its .shx, .dbf, and preferably .prj companions), KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, GeoPackage (.gpkg), and CSV plot centres. Preserve unique plot identifiers and a valid coordinate reference system. Polygon inputs define their own core boundaries; CSV centre records need shape dimensions and, when needed, an explicit CRS. Do not interpret a centre-only CSV as an arbitrary polygon boundary.

Shapefile example (existing polygon boundaries):

fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_SHP_Plots" `
    --sensor_mode ALS `
    --sampling imported `
    --plot_file "G:\Survey\permanent_plots.shp" `
    --buffer 5
Parameter Function / definition Configuration guidance --plot_file Existing SHP polygon dataset Include shapefile companion files and a valid CRS --sampling imported Use authored plot geometry Does not resample locations --buffer Processing margin around imported core 5 m in this example; preserves polygon as core --out_dir Published collection workspace Use a fresh directory --in_path, --sensor_mode Source survey and sensor Keep consistent with survey

KML example (existing plot boundaries):

fastgc gis `
    --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
    --out_dir "G:\FASTGC_BR01_KML_Plots" `

docs.title: 3.9.1 Product lineage
docs.text:
1. FAST-GIS: survey → sampled polygon cores → buffered LAZ + per-plot metadata + collection manifest.
  2. FAST_GC: classify ground/non-ground returns in each plot.
  3. FAST_DEM: interpolate terrain elevation from suitable ground support.
  4. FAST_DSM: estimate surface elevation from appropriate returns when requested.
  5. FAST_CHM: estimate height above terrain; method-dependent surface processing.
  6. FAST_NORMALIZED: express point Z relative to terrain.
  7. FAST_TERRAIN: derive terrain metrics from the DEM.
  8. FAST_STRUCTURE: derive vertical and geometric forest descriptors.
  9. FAST_ITD / FAST_TREECLOUDS: tree detection and individual-tree extraction, when requested and appropriately configured.
  10. FAST_CHANGE: compare matched products from multiple surveys, not meaningful from a single-date plot alone.

This is a conceptual lineage, not a claim that every downstream product depends only on the three initial rasters or that every product was successfully executed in the demonstrated command.

docs.title: 3.15.5 Reader exercise: reproduce the Plot 005 interpretation
docs.text:
After running the random circular clipping and managed plots-run commands in §§3.3 and 3.9, open ALS_plots/Plot_005/Clip_Plot_005.json. Check the plot ID, point_extent, core_geometry, buffer_m, core_points, and points_written. Confirm that plots_manifest.json identifies this plot and its LAZ file. Next compare Figures 3.1–3.3: explain the difference between absolute elevation, ground class, and normalized height. Finally examine the terrain, structure, vertical-layer, and geometry figures presented once in their respective sections and answer:

  1. Where are the steepest cells in Plot 005, and do they correspond to high or low TPI?
  2. Which cells have the tallest returns? Do they also have high canopy cover?
  3. Where is vertical diversity high or low, and does point density support that interpretation?
  4. Do linearity and planarity maps describe the same spatial features?
  5. Which findings are constrained by the 15 m core boundary or the available return density?

Use the companion CSV for numeric range checks, and do not assume that colors can be compared across metrics without reading each legend. The exercise deliberately uses the same Plot 005 throughout.

docs.title: 3.16 Summary and transition
docs.text: FAST-GIS turns spatially extensive ALS/ULS/TLS surveys into reproducible, machine-readable plot collections. The principal scientific safeguards are coverage-aware selection, explicit projected coordinates, separate core and buffer geometries, complete per-plot provenance, and managed downstream product publication. Plot 005 demonstrates how ground-classified and normalized points can support DEM/DSM/CHM surfaces, terrain metrics, and detailed vertical/geometric forest structure. The next chapter develops the ground-classification algorithm and its sensor-specific behavior in detail.

docs.title: 3.17 Literature foundations and metric definitions
docs.text: The purpose of the references below is to explain scientific foundations and interpretation. A citation to an established algorithm is not a claim that FAST-GC copied that algorithm. Implementation-specific definitions below were checked against the bundled FAST-GC/src/fastgc/structure.py and FAST-GC/src/fastgc/gis/gis_cli.py source snapshot; terrain citations provide context, and the exact terrain kernels must be checked separately before describing an individual definition as FAST-GC-specific.

docs.title: 3.17.1 Reproducible metric definitions in FAST_STRUCTURE
docs.text:
The following metrics use height-normalized LiDAR returns. The source implementation distinguishes all valid returns from vegetation returns selected using a configured minimum height threshold. Vertical metrics divide the height profile into intervals and describe the distribution of returns among those intervals.

FAST_STRUCTURE metric Implementation-specific definition Output and interpretive use Literature basis canopy_cover Proportion of all valid returns exceeding the canopy-height threshold. Fraction of all finite returns exceeding canopy threshold; return-based cover proxy, not independently calibrated crown area [R3], [R4] n_points_all Number of all valid returns in a raster cell. All-point support per cell [R4] n_points Number of returns meeting the minimum vegetation-height threshold. Vegetation-height point support [R4] point_density Number of eligible vegetation returns per square metre. Vegetation returns/m² [R4] z_mean Average normalized vegetation-return height. Mean vegetation-return height, m [R4] z_sd Population standard deviation of normalized vegetation-return heights. Height variability, m [R4] z_p50, z_p95, z_p99 np.percentile of vegetation heights Median, upper-canopy and near-maximum return heights, m [R4] vertical_entropy = FHD Shannon diversity of LiDAR returns distributed across occupied vertical height intervals. Shannon entropy of occupied height bins [R1], [R2], [R3] vertical_evenness = VCI Vertical entropy normalized by the number of occupied height intervals. Normalized by occupied-bin count, not total possible bins [R1], [R2] vertical_richness Count of vertical height intervals containing at least one return. Number of occupied height bins [R2], [R3] vertical_effective_layers Effective number of occupied height layers derived from Shannon entropy. Entropy-equivalent number of height layers [R1], [R2] vertical_simpson Diversity of returns among height intervals, using a Simpson-type index. Vertical diversity; 0 for one occupied layer [R2] vertical_dominance Largest proportion of returns concentrated in one occupied height interval. Fraction in the dominant occupied height bin [R2] vertical_occupancy_fraction Proportion of height intervals occupied between the lowest and highest occupied intervals. Fraction of within-profile bins containing returns [R2] vertical_gap_count Count of internal empty-bin runs between first/last occupied bins Number of internal vertical discontinuities [R2], [R3] vertical_gap_fraction Proportion of empty intervals within the occupied vertical span. Within-profile vertical emptiness [R2] max_vertical_gap_m Height in metres of the longest internal empty interval sequence. Maximum vertical discontinuity, m [R2] first_return_fraction Fraction of vegetation points whose return_number==1 First-return share of vegetation returns [R4] multi_return_fraction Fraction of vegetation points whose return_number>1 Later-return share; not fraction of pulses producing multiple returns [R4] z_skewness Third central moment / population SD³; 0 for zero SD Asymmetry of height distribution [R4] z_kurtosis Fourth central moment / population SD⁴ minus 3; 0 for zero SD Excess kurtosis of heights [R4]

Important correction to common interpretations: VCI in this implementation is the Shannon entropy normalized by the logarithm of occupied vertical bins, and multi_return_fraction is computed as the proportion of points with return_number>1. It should not be described as the fraction of pulses that produced multiple returns. canopy_cover is return-based, so it should not be equated with field-measured crown projection without calibration.

docs.text:
FAST_STRUCTURE computes robust weighted covariance within eligible raster cells. It uses a coordinate median and distance-based robust weights to reduce the influence of unusually distant points. Covariance descriptors summarize the spread of points along three principal spatial directions; they do not by themselves identify biological classes.

Metric Implementation-specific definition Interpretation Literature linearity Extent to which points follow one principal spatial direction. Line-like local 3D arrangement [R8] planarity Extent to which points occupy a locally planar arrangement. Planar arrangement [R8] sphericity Extent to which local points are distributed similarly across three spatial directions. Isotropic / volumetric spread [R8] anisotropy Strength of directional differences in local point geometry. Directional imbalance [R8] omnivariance Combined spread of the local point distribution along three principal directions. Overall covariance-volume scale; units depend on eigenvalue units [R8] surface_variation Relative contribution of the smallest covariance eigenvalue, indicating deviation from planarity. Local departure from planarity [R8] eigenentropy Diversity of normalized covariance eigenvalues; describes geometric disorder. Distribution of normalized covariance eigenvalues [R1], [R8] normal_inclination_deg Inclination of local fitted normal from vertical, degrees Inclination of local fitted normal from vertical, degrees [R8]

These descriptors summarize the spatial arrangement of the returns in the cell. They are not validated biological class probabilities for stems, branches, or leaves.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Cross-Platform Installation, Configuration, and Performance
Chapter 2 — Installation, Configuration, and Performance Optimization
docs.text: Documentation release: FAST-GC v0.2.1 Scope: installation, environment checks, and FAST_GC-only speed tests. Detailed FAST_DEM, FAST_CHM, and other product validation is reserved for their respective chapters.

docs.title: 2.1 Installation overview
docs.text:
FAST-GC is a Python command-line application for ground classification of airborne (ALS), UAV (ULS), and terrestrial (TLS) LiDAR data. Release 0.2.1 declares Python 3.12–3.14 compatibility. The tested installation environments used Python 3.12.15 on Windows and Ubuntu WSL2, and Python 3.13 in Google Colab. Use an isolated environment; avoid changing your operating system's Python interpreter.

Installation pathway System Evidence Conda environment + PyPI Windows 11 Pro Installation, pip check, fastgc-check, CLI and imports passed Python venv + PyPI Windows 11 Pro Installation, dependencies, CLI and imports passed GitHub editable installation Windows 11 Pro Editable build, dependencies, CLI and source import passed uv + PyPI Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS on WSL2 Installation, 23 dependency packages, checks and CLI passed PyPI in Google Colab Hosted Linux, Python 3.13 Installation and an ALS run completed previously Native Ubuntu (not WSL2) — Not independently tested macOS Intel / Apple Silicon — Guidance only; not independently tested

docs.title: Reference hardware and software
docs.text:
Property Tested configuration Workstation Dell G16 7620 CPU Intel Core i9-12900H, 14 physical cores / 20 logical processors Host RAM Approximately 31.69 GiB Windows Windows 11 Pro Linux Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS on WSL2; Linux-reported available RAM approximately 27.4 GiB during the benchmark Windows and WSL2 Python 3.12.15 FAST-GC 0.2.1 Reference point cloud Site5 ALS, approximately 3.5 million points; source Site 15 in Jin et al. (2020)

A GPU is not required for the tested core FAST_GC workflow. RAM and disk needs depend on point count, density, tile dimensions, and concurrency; 16 GiB or more is a practical recommendation for substantial datasets, not a formal minimum.

docs.title: 2.2 Windows: Conda + PyPI
docs.text:
Open PowerShell with Conda available. The following block creates an isolated environment, installs the pinned release, and checks it.

conda create -n fastgc python=3.12 pip -y
conda activate fastgc
python -m pip install fastgc==0.2.1
python -m pip check
fastgc-check
fastgc --version
fastgc --help

Expected version: fastgc 0.2.1. If the installation command succeeds but fastgc is not recognized, check that the correct environment is active with conda info --envs and Get-Command fastgc.

One-paste PowerShell installation (no activation required):

conda create -n fastgc python=3.12 pip -y; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Conda environment failed' }; conda run -n fastgc python -m pip install fastgc==0.2.1; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'FAST-GC installation failed' }; conda run -n fastgc python -m pip check; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency check failed' }; conda run -n fastgc fastgc-check; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'FAST-GC check failed' }; conda run -n fastgc fastgc --version

docs.title: 2.3 Windows: Python venv + PyPI
docs.text:
This method requires an installed Python 3.12 interpreter accessible through the Windows Python launcher.

py -3.12 --version
py -3.12 -m venv "$HOME\fastgc_venv"
& "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip install fastgc==0.2.1
& "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip check
& "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\fastgc-check.exe"
& "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\fastgc.exe" --version

Using the environment executables directly avoids PowerShell execution-policy issues. To activate interactively when permitted:

& "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1"

One-paste PowerShell installation:

py -3.12 -m venv "$HOME\fastgc_venv"; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'venv creation failed' }; & "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip install fastgc==0.2.1; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Install failed' }; & "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m pip check; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency check failed' }; & "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\fastgc-check.exe"; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Diagnostic failed' }; & "$HOME\fastgc_venv\Scripts\fastgc.exe" --version

docs.title: 2.4 Windows: GitHub source / editable installation
docs.text:
Use editable installation if you plan to inspect or modify FAST-GC source code. The pinned release tag provides a more reproducible baseline than an unspecified development branch.

conda create -n fastgc_source python=3.12 pip -y
conda activate fastgc_source
git clone https://github.com/nadeemfareed/FAST-GC.git
cd FAST-GC
git checkout v0.2.1
python -m pip install -e .
python -m pip check
fastgc-check
fastgc --version
python -c "import fastgc; print(fastgc.__file__)"
git rev-parse HEAD

The Windows editable-installation test succeeded against the repository default branch reporting version 0.2.1; the exact tested commit was not independently recorded. The explicit git checkout v0.2.1 above is a reproducibility recommendation, not a claim that the test used that tag.

One-paste PowerShell source installation:

conda create -n fastgc_source python=3.12 pip -y; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Conda failed' }; git clone https://github.com/nadeemfareed/FAST-GC.git "$HOME\FAST-GC"; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Clone failed; check whether target already exists' }; git -C "$HOME\FAST-GC" checkout v0.2.1; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Checkout failed' }; conda run -n fastgc_source python -m pip install -e "$HOME\FAST-GC"; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Install failed' }; conda run -n fastgc_source fastgc-check; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Diagnostic failed' }; conda run -n fastgc_source fastgc --version

The one-paste command assumes $HOME\FAST-GC does not already exist.

docs.title: 2.5 Ubuntu 22.04 and WSL2: uv installation
docs.text:
Ubuntu 22.04's system Python 3.10 is below FAST-GC v0.2.1's minimum. Do not replace system Python. Install Python 3.12 into an isolated uv environment instead.

From Windows PowerShell, enter Ubuntu:

wsl -d Ubuntu-22.04

Then in the Ubuntu shell:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
uv python install 3.12
uv venv --python 3.12 "$HOME/fastgc_env"
uv pip install --python "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/python" fastgc==0.2.1
uv pip check --python "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/python"
"$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/fastgc-check"
"$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/fastgc" --version

One-paste installation directly from Windows PowerShell (requires WSL2 and Ubuntu-22.04 already installed):

wsl -d Ubuntu-22.04 -- bash -lc 'set -e; export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"; if ! command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh; fi; uv python install 3.12; uv venv --python 3.12 "$HOME/fastgc_env"; uv pip install --python "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/python" fastgc==0.2.1; uv pip check --python "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/python"; "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/fastgc-check"; "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/fastgc" --version'

Windows paths such as C:\data\Site5.las are accessed from WSL2 as /mnt/c/data/Site5.las. For tiled workloads, using Linux-native output storage under $HOME is a practical starting point; the speed impact of storage location was not isolated in these tests.

docs.title: 2.6 Google Colab
docs.text:
Run the following in Colab notebook cells:

%pip install fastgc==0.2.1

import sys, importlib.metadata
print(sys.version)
print(importlib.metadata.version('fastgc'))

!fastgc-check
!fastgc --version
!fastgc --help

For input stored in Google Drive:

from google.colab import drive
drive.mount('/content/drive')

A FAST_GC-only example, assuming the file exists:

!fastgc --in_path '/content/drive/MyDrive/Site5.las' --out_dir '/content/FASTGC_OUTPUT' --sensor_mode ALS --workflow run --products FAST_GC

Colab CPU and memory allocations vary. /content is temporary; copy results to persistent storage before the runtime ends. A GPU runtime is not required for the tested FAST_GC workflow.

docs.title: 2.7 Local Jupyter Notebook and JupyterLab
docs.text:
Install Jupyter in the same environment as FAST-GC, then register the kernel:

conda activate fastgc
python -m pip install jupyterlab ipykernel
python -m ipykernel install --user --name fastgc --display-name 'Python (FAST-GC)'
jupyter lab

Select Python (FAST-GC) as the notebook kernel. In an existing notebook, %pip install fastgc==0.2.1 targets the current kernel. Restart the kernel after installation if necessary.

Verify the active interpreter:

import sys, importlib.metadata
print('Kernel Python:', sys.executable)
print('FAST-GC:', importlib.metadata.version('fastgc'))

For robust multiprocessing, execute the FAST-GC CLI as a subprocess instead of embedding worker creation directly in notebook code:

import os, sys, subprocess, time
from pathlib import Path

exe = Path(sys.executable).parent / ('fastgc.exe' if os.name == 'nt' else 'fastgc')
input_file = r'C:\path\to\Site5.las'   # change to your real path
output_dir = r'C:\path\to\FASTGC_NOTEBOOK_TEST'
cmd = [str(exe), '--in_path', input_file, '--out_dir', output_dir,
       '--sensor_mode', 'ALS', '--workflow', 'tile-run-merge',
       '--products', 'FAST_GC', '--tile_size_m', '140',
       '--buffer_m', '4', '--jobs', '8', '--joblib_backend', 'loky',
       '--joblib_pre_dispatch', '2*n_jobs', '--cleanup_tiles']
env = os.environ.copy()
for k in ('OMP_NUM_THREADS', 'OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS', 'MKL_NUM_THREADS', 'NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS'):
    env[k] = '1'
env['LAZRS_NUM_THREADS'] = '2'
t0 = time.perf_counter()
subprocess.run(cmd, env=env, check=True)
print(f'Elapsed: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s')

For Linux notebook kernels, replace the Windows paths with Linux paths.

docs.title: 2.8 macOS installation (not independently tested)
docs.text:
With Python 3.12 installed:

python3.12 -m venv "$HOME/fastgc_env"
source "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/activate"
python -m pip install fastgc==0.2.1
python -m pip check
fastgc-check
fastgc --version

Availability of compatible binary distributions may differ between Intel and Apple Silicon. If source compilation is required, inspect the specific build error before installing compilers or Rust tooling. This chapter does not claim verified macOS compatibility.

docs.title: 2.9 Standard FAST_GC command interface
docs.text:
The same CLI argument names apply across Windows and Linux. PowerShell is the standard presentation style in this book; Linux equivalents use Bash syntax.

Minimal PowerShell test (replace paths):

fastgc `
  --in_path 'C:\path\to\small_als_sample.las' `
  --out_dir 'C:\path\to\FASTGC_SMOKE_OUTPUT' `
  --sensor_mode ALS `
  --workflow run `
  --products FAST_GC

A small sample checks functional execution, not optimal performance. The sample path is illustrative, not a bundled test asset.

Tested Windows speed configuration:

conda activate fastgc
$env:OMP_NUM_THREADS = '1'
$env:OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = '1'
$env:MKL_NUM_THREADS = '1'
$env:NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS = '1'
$env:LAZRS_NUM_THREADS = '2'
$IN = 'C:\path\to\Site5.las'
$OUT = 'C:\path\to\FASTGC_SPEED_TEST'
Measure-Command {
    fastgc `
      --in_path $IN `
      --out_dir $OUT `
      --sensor_mode ALS `
      --workflow tile-run-merge `
      --products FAST_GC `
      --tile_size_m 140 `
      --buffer_m 4 `
      --jobs 8 `
      --joblib_backend loky `
      --joblib_pre_dispatch '2*n_jobs' `
      --cleanup_tiles
}

Equivalent Ubuntu FAST_GC-only test:

source "$HOME/fastgc_env/bin/activate"
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1 LAZRS_NUM_THREADS=2
time fastgc \
  --in_path '/path/to/Site5.las' \
  --out_dir "$HOME/FASTGC_SPEED_TEST" \
  --sensor_mode ALS \
  --workflow tile-run-merge \
  --products FAST_GC \
  --tile_size_m 140 \
  --buffer_m 4 \
  --jobs 8 \
  --joblib_backend loky \
  --joblib_pre_dispatch '2*n_jobs' \
  --cleanup_tiles

For reproducible timing, use a fresh output directory. The correct FAST-GC v0.2.1 tile buffer flag is --buffer_m, not --tile_buffer_m. The available workflows and flags should always be checked using fastgc --help for the installed release.

docs.title: Worker scaling on the reference Windows workstation
docs.text:
Site5 ALS, FAST_GC-only, 140 m tiles, 4 m buffer, tile-run-merge:

Workers Wall time (s) Speedup versus 1 worker 1 2085.38 1.00× 2 1185.86 1.76× 4 755.59 2.76× 6 633.45 3.29× 8 600.87 3.47× 10 Approximately 903 Approximately 2.31×

Eight workers were fastest among the tested configurations on this workstation. Ten workers performed worse, illustrating scheduling, memory, or I/O contention beyond the practical optimum. Individual runs were measured; confidence intervals and repeat-run statistics were not established.

docs.title: Tile geometry
docs.text:
Tile size Buffer Workers Tiles Runtime 140 m 4 m 8 16 600.87 s 50 m 3 m 8 100 830.39 s

The 50 m configuration was approximately 38.2% slower. Buffer width also changed, so this is not a controlled tile-size-only experiment. Smaller tiles can reduce per-task memory while increasing scheduling and intermediate-file overhead; larger tiles do the reverse.

docs.title: Ubuntu WSL2 execution observation
docs.text:
A completed WSL2 Site5 run used 140 m tiles, 4 m buffer, eight loky workers, and requested FAST_GC, FAST_DEM, and FAST_CHM. It completed 16/16 tiles without reported failures, with FAST_GC classification taking approximately 5 min 04 s and full shell wall time 338.395 s (5 min 38 s). The merged FAST_GC point count was 3,503,054. The application's internal FAST-GC total was 312.72 s.

The earlier Windows FAST_GC-only run took 600.87 s, so the observed Linux wall time was 1.78× shorter in ratio terms (43.7% less elapsed time). This is preliminary cross-platform evidence, not a controlled OS-only speed comparison: requested products, runtime conditions, and filesystem behavior differed. A repeated FAST_GC-only run on both platforms is needed to attribute the difference to the operating system.

docs.title: Practical optimization rules
docs.text:
• Start with a worker count appropriate for CPU cores and available RAM; do not assume more workers are always faster.
  • Use process-level parallelism (--joblib_backend loky) for the documented benchmark configuration.
  • Limit common numerical-library thread pools to avoid oversubscription when running multiple workers.
  • Use --joblib_pre_dispatch '2*n_jobs' as the tested dispatch setting; it controls queued tasks, not the number of worker processes.
  • Choose tile size and buffer based on dataset geometry and memory requirements; avoid shrinking buffers solely to improve runtime.
  • Prefer fast local storage for intermediate tiles; under WSL2, Linux-native output directories are a reasonable starting point.
  • Keep sensor mode consistent with acquisition type: ALS, ULS, or TLS. A faster mode is not automatically a scientifically appropriate mode.
  • Record wall time, input point count, tile count, worker count, environment, and failure count.

docs.title: 2.11 Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely explanation Action No matching distribution found Unsupported Python or unavailable compatible build Check python --version; use isolated Python 3.12 fastgc not recognized Wrong environment or PATH Activate environment or invoke its fastgc executable directly PowerShell blocks Activate.ps1 Script execution policy Call the venv's executables directly; no policy change required Ubuntu Python 3.10 System interpreter below supported version Use uv python install 3.12 and an isolated uv venv No module named pip inside uv venv pip may not be installed in uv environment Use uv pip install --python ... unrecognized arguments: --tile_buffer_m 4 Invalid flag in v0.2.1 Use --buffer_m 4 fastgc-check reports missing dependency Incomplete or conflicting installation Run pip check; retry in clean environment Source build fails Missing compatible wheel or native toolchain Inspect compiler/build error; install only necessary build tools Out-of-memory / worker failures Too many jobs or oversized tiles Reduce --jobs and/or tile size Poor scaling at high --jobs Scheduling, I/O or thread contention Benchmark fewer workers with fixed input/settings Jupyter kernel cannot import FAST-GC Notebook kernel points to another Python Register/select correct ipykernel; inspect sys.executable Jupyter multiprocessing hangs Worker process interaction with notebook kernel Run CLI via subprocess.run(...) Colab runtime disconnects Session lifetime or memory limits Reduce workload and save outputs to persistent storage WSL2 cannot find C:\... path Windows path used in Linux Convert to /mnt/c/...

Important: A passing fastgc-check verifies environment readiness, not classification accuracy. A completed CLI test verifies execution, not the scientific validity of every downstream product.

docs.title: 2.12 Reproducibility checklist
docs.text:
For each published installation or performance result, record:

  1. FAST-GC version, package source, and Git commit where relevant.
  2. Python version, environment manager, and installed dependency builds.
  3. Operating system, architecture, CPU, logical cores, and available RAM.
  4. Sensor mode, input LAS/LAZ file, point count, and storage location.
  5. Workflow, requested products, tile size, buffer, and worker count.
  6. Joblib backend, dispatch settings, and thread environment variables.
  7. Tiling/classification/merging durations and total wall time.
  8. Successful, skipped, and failed tiles; final output point count.
  9. Whether the benchmark was repeated, and which conditions were matched.

docs.title: 2.13 Chapter summary
docs.text:
FAST-GC v0.2.1 was successfully installed and initialized using Windows Conda, Windows Python venv, Windows GitHub editable installation, Ubuntu WSL2 with uv, and Google Colab. Python 3.12 and isolated environments provide a reproducible starting point. PowerShell is the standard interface for Windows readers, while Bash and notebook equivalents preserve the same CLI configuration.

The reference Windows Site5 FAST_GC benchmark reached its fastest observed runtime with eight workers, 140 m tiles, and a 4 m buffer. The completed Ubuntu WSL2 execution demonstrated a substantially shorter observed wall time, but a controlled FAST_GC-only cross-platform comparison remains necessary. Readers should benchmark their own hardware, avoid thread oversubscription, and preserve consistent workflow parameters.

Further reading: FAST-GC source repository, FAST-GC on PyPI, and the FAST-GC preprint.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — FAST-GC ground classification, core products, and wall-to-wall LiDAR mapping
docs.text: Study design: a complete airborne laser scanning (ALS) survey for measured examples; operational workflows also apply to uncrewed laser scanning (ULS) and terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), with sensor-specific tuning. Scope: reproducible processing and deliverables, not the mathematical ground-filtering algorithm. Hydrological and terrain analysis are covered in the next chapter.

docs.title: 4.1 From classified points to continuous maps
docs.text:
FAST-GC processes LAS/LAZ surveys through ground classification, optional height normalization, and raster surface generation. The core output is a classified point cloud; DEM, DSM, normalized cloud, and CHM are direct products of the processing pipeline. Terrain derivatives, hydrology, canopy structure, and tree-level analysis are downstream applications, not synonyms for ground classification.

Product Meaning Typical use Notes FAST_GC Ground/non-ground classified point cloud Terrain support, quality control Preserve original survey metadata and inspect class counts FAST_DEM Digital Elevation Model: ground elevation Terrain reference A grid's no-data cells are not zero elevation FAST_DSM Digital Surface Model: upper observed surface Surface/canopy representation Includes buildings and other above-ground objects where present FAST_NORMALIZED Point cloud expressed as height relative to DEM Canopy and vertical-profile analysis Height depends on DEM quality and sampling FAST_CHM Canopy Height Model: modeled height above terrain Canopy surface and tree applications Different reconstruction methods may give different surfaces FAST_TERRAIN, FAST_STRUCTURE, etc. Downstream analytical products Terrain/hydrology/forest characterization Covered separately to avoid duplication

Wall-to-wall refers to a spatially continuous mapped study footprint assembled from tiled processing. It does not mean every raster cell must contain an observation: no-data gaps and sparse point support remain possible. The processing buffer provides neighboring context; the intended tile core must govern the final mosaic to avoid duplicate edge observations.

docs.title: 4.2 Processing modes and their use
docs.text:
Workflow Intended operation Appropriate situation run Process an input directly Single, manageable file without tiling tile-only Generate reusable spatial tiles Inspect coverage or stage later processing tile-run Tile and process Keep processed tiles for inspection or later merge tile-run-merge Tile, process, and merge Standard wall-to-wall survey workflow merge Merge existing processed tiles Complete an interrupted or deliberately staged workflow derive-only Derive products from an existing processed root Avoid redoing successful ground classification

A workflow is not a product. For example, tile-run-merge can request FAST_GC alone for a benchmark or request classification, DEM, normalization, DSM, and multiple CHMs in one execution. Products are requested with --products; CHM variants are specified with --chm_methods.

docs.title: 4.3 Full-survey ALS example: BR01
docs.text:
The demonstration uses the complete BR01 ALS file, not the circular Plot 005 subset from Chapter 3. The file was provided and processed on Windows:

G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz

docs.title: 4.3.0 Before running: verify the active CLI
docs.text:
Run in Windows PowerShell (not CMD or Python). The backtick ` must be the final character on each continued line: no spaces after it. Paste the complete command block, rather than typing >> prompts shown by PowerShell. Use conda activate fastgc to select the intended environment.

conda activate fastgc
python -c "import fastgc; print(fastgc.__file__)"
fastgc --help

Check that the help lists tile-run-merge, derive-only, and the exact options in the chosen command. These preflight commands do not process LiDAR. The FAST-GC source archive used to review these examples is dated 2026-10-08; a later installed release may differ. In particular, the successful BR01 individual-tree export depended on local fixes to the installed treeclouds.py that have not yet been established as part of the public release.

docs.title: 4.3.1 FAST_GC-only baseline
docs.text:
fastgc `
  --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
  --out_dir "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\BR01_FASTGC_140m" `
  --sensor_mode ALS `
  --workflow tile-run-merge `
  --products FAST_GC `
  --tile_size_m 140 `
  --buffer_m 4 `
  --jobs 8
Parameter Function Configuration guidance --in_path LAS/LAZ file or input directory Must exist; this path is specific to the BR01 workstation --out_dir Output root Use a new directory for every independent benchmark --sensor_mode ALS Select airborne sensor pathway Use ULS or TLS only for the corresponding survey --workflow tile-run-merge Create, classify, and merge tiles Appropriate for continuous survey mapping --products FAST_GC Classification only Isolates ground-processing runtime --tile_size_m 140 Tile width in metres Previously benchmarked; not a universal optimum --buffer_m 4 Processing context around each tile, metres Evaluate seams and point duplication at tile edges --jobs 8 Parallel tile workers Adjust to available memory and CPU; default 0 auto-selects workers

Observed result: 9/9 tiles classified and merged, 12,531,911 points reported in merged FAST_GC output, and 7 min 23.04 s end-to-end. The reported tiling stage took 26.97 s and merge 20.72 s. These are processing metrics, not ground-classification accuracy measurements.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Standard end-to-end command: ground, DEM, normalization, DSM, and CHM
docs.text:
fastgc `
  --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m.laz" `
  --out_dir "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\BR01_ALL_PRODUCTS" `
  --sensor_mode ALS `
  --workflow tile-run-merge `
  --products FAST_GC FAST_DEM FAST_NORMALIZED FAST_DSM FAST_CHM `
  --tile_size_m 140 `
  --buffer_m 4 `
  --jobs 8 `
  --grid_res 1.0 `
  --dem_method min `
  --chm_methods p2r p99 tin pitfree spikefree `
    percentile:pitfree:pct=5 `
    percentile_top:pitfree:low=5 `
    percentile_band:pitfree:low=2:high=8
Parameter Function Configuration guidance --products Requests point-cloud and raster deliverables FAST_NORMALIZED requires terrain support; DSM is included for spike-free routing --grid_res 1.0 Raster cell size, in metres 1 m used for all uploaded BR01 rasters; smaller cells need more point support --dem_method min DEM grid method Minimum classified ground elevation; alternatives: max, mean, nearest, idw --chm_methods Multiple CHM outputs in one run The six supported plain multi-method names are p2r, p99, tin, pitfree, spikefree, csf_chm; CSF is omitted here percentile:pitfree:pct=5 Keep normalized points at or below 5 m, then apply pit-free reconstruction Height-limited surface; pct=5 is not a 5th-percentile statistic in this version percentile_top:pitfree:low=5 Keep points at or above 5 m, then apply pit-free reconstruction Useful for upper-canopy support; sparse gaps may remain percentile_band:pitfree:low=2:high=8 Keep points between 2 and 8 m, then apply pit-free reconstruction Height-stratum product; never interpret as full canopy height

CLI compatibility note. The installed CLI advertises adaptive_pitfree for --chm_method, but the multi-target parser rejects it under --chm_methods. It is excluded from the runnable example. Command preconditions: activate the fastgc environment, verify the input path exists, and choose a new output directory. These examples are for the specific BR01 path and should not be copied unchanged to another computer.

docs.title: 4.4 Tiled mapping: footprint, buffers, merge, and performance
docs.text:
The operational sequence is source files → tiles with processing context → classified tiles → optional surface products → merged survey products. For contiguous survey tiles, merging is necessary to provide a single study-area deliverable. Tile processing can be retained when individual tile quality control or staged recomputation is required.

The nominal tile size affects the number of tasks; the buffer affects the volume of duplicated processing context. Small tiles may increase task-launch and buffer overhead; large tiles may increase peak per-worker memory. More workers do not guarantee higher throughput when memory bandwidth or disk access becomes limiting.

docs.text:
The CLI accepts a directory through --in_path; --recursive enables nested-directory scanning. A directory input is useful when an acquisition is delivered as several adjacent LAS/LAZ files. First check that all files share a compatible horizontal coordinate reference system, elevation units, and survey metadata. A directory of unrelated surveys should not be treated as one contiguous wall-to-wall area.

The following example is intentionally a template, not an executable BR01 command; it requires the reader to substitute a real existing directory:

  --out_dir "$surveyFolder\FASTGC_WALL_TO_WALL" `
  --sensor_mode ALS `
  --workflow tile-run-merge `
  --products FAST_GC FAST_DEM FAST_NORMALIZED FAST_CHM `
  --tile_size_m 140 `
  --buffer_m 4 `
  --jobs 8 `
  --grid_res 1.0 `

docs.title: 4.5 ALS, ULS, and TLS: operational distinctions
docs.text:
Consideration ALS ULS TLS Acquisition geometry Top-down airborne returns Low-altitude airborne returns, often denser and more variable Side-looking and multi-scan ground perspective Ground support Often spatially distributed beneath canopy gaps Highly dependent on flight pattern and canopy penetration Can be abundant near scanner but occluded behind vegetation and objects Tiling Survey-scale tiling generally appropriate Adapt tile size to density and flight overlap Start conservatively with dense scans; watch memory and per-tile point counts Buffer Required to stabilize tile-edge context Evaluate across dense flight strips and edges Consider scan occlusion and local neighborhood support DEM/CHM Typical forest and terrain products Suitable where ground coverage supports normalization Surface rasters may have severe occlusion/voids; inspect rather than assume full coverage Validation Ground control / independently labeled points Ground control and flight-strip consistency Scanner geometry, scan positions, and independent terrain reference

docs.title: 4.6 DEM: resolution and interpolation
docs.text:
A Digital Elevation Model is an estimate of terrain elevation on a regular grid. The chosen grid spacing determines how much detail can be represented, but a fine cell size does not create ground returns where none were observed. FAST-GC 0.2.1 exposes min, max, mean, nearest, and idw as --dem_method options.

DEM method Interpretation Practical caution min Minimum classified ground elevation contributing to a cell Sensitive to low outliers or misclassified points max Maximum contributing ground elevation May emphasize high points in sloping cells mean Mean ground elevation Smooths within-cell variation nearest Nearest-sample interpolation Local abrupt transitions possible idw Inverse-distance-weighted interpolation Neighborhood and distance assumptions affect surfaces

For BR01, the supplied DEM was produced at 1 m using the min setting. To compare methods or 0.5 m, 1 m, and 2 m grids, keep the same ground-classified input and evaluate terrain artifacts, missing cells, and runtime. Those comparisons have not been measured in the supplied BR01 raster set, so no superiority ranking is claimed.

Figure 4.1. BR01 DEM, DSM, P2R CHM and pit-free CHM derived from the supplied GeoTIFFs. All four panels are clipped to the same valid DSM footprint for direct spatial comparison. DEM elevations are unchanged inside the footprint; outside cells are hidden only for visualization. Elevation and canopy-height color scales are separate. White indicates excluded or missing cells.

docs.title: 4.7 CHM variants and percentile families
docs.text:
The CHM methods reconstruct canopy height from available observations and the terrain reference. They are not interchangeable algorithms; their differences should be evaluated against point density, canopy gaps, crown boundaries, and independent canopy-height evidence.

CHM method Working interpretation Potential strengths / cautions p2r Point-to-raster canopy surface Direct and simple; can contain sampling pits p99 High-percentile canopy-height surface Reduces sensitivity to isolated maxima; can suppress narrow crown peaks tin Triangulated surface Interpolates between supports; can bridge real gaps pitfree Multi-layer pit-free canopy reconstruction Can reduce pits; evaluate crown-edge smoothing and gap filling spikefree DSM-first spike-free reconstruction May reduce spikes; depends on DSM routing and ground reference percentile Fareed (2026) height-filtered canopy reconstruction: retain points at or below pct height This implementation's pct is a height threshold in metres, not a statistical percentile percentile_top Fareed (2026) upper-canopy point selection: retain points at or above low Feed the retained upper points into a primary CHM algorithm such as pitfree percentile_band Fareed (2026) height-band point selection: retain points between low and high Reconstruct the selected stratum; it is not a full-height CHM

docs.title: Fareed (2026): height-selective CHM reconstruction
docs.text:
The Fareed (2026) percentile family adds a point-selection stage before the primary canopy-surface reconstruction. In the supplied FAST-GC implementation, selection is performed on the point-cloud Z height (typically height-normalized canopy points); the selected points are then processed by the named primary CHM method. This distinction matters: the implementation does not calculate a statistical 5th percentile from the height distribution when the selector is written as pct=5.

Selector expression Exact current selection rule Subsequent reconstruction Intended interpretation percentile:pitfree:pct=5 Keep z <= 5 m Pit-free CHM on retained points Lower-height-limited surface; canopy maxima above 5 m are excluded percentile_top:pitfree:low=5 Keep z >= 5 m Pit-free CHM on retained points Upper-canopy-focused surface retaining the actual height of selected points percentile_band:pitfree:low=2:high=8 Keep 2 m <= z <= 8 m Pit-free CHM on retained points Height-stratified surface, not whole-canopy maximum

Algorithmic sequence: normalized canopy points → apply Fareed (2026) height selector → run primary CHM reconstruction (pitfree in these examples) → rasterize and merge. Thresholds refer to the Z values used by the implementation and should not be confused with quantile percentages. The terminology percentile family is retained as the software's method name; the threshold behavior is stated explicitly for reproducibility.

csf_chm is supported but deliberately excluded from this comparison. adaptive_pitfree appears in the primary CLI choices but was rejected by the installed multi-target parser; it is not listed as a working multi-target command.

docs.title: 4.8 CHM-based crown segmentation and individual-tree detection
docs.text: A canopy height model is a height surface, not an individual-tree map. FAST_ITD delineates candidate crowns from a CHM, produces a crown-label raster and treetop locations, and exports a combined crown shapefile. FAST_TREECLOUDS subsequently uses the crown delineation to assign points in a normalized LAS to individual tree segments. These are distinct stages: a polygon is not itself a 3D tree point cloud.

docs.title: 4.8.1 Methods exposed by FAST-GC 0.2.1
docs.text: The installed CLI advertises placeholder, lmf, watershed, adaptive_watershed, yun2021, dalponte2016, li2012, and csp. These are available CLI choices, not evidence that every method is CHM-only, equally mature, or equally accurate. The BR01 full-plot experiment selected yun2021 after user visual comparison; no reference-based accuracy ranking was established. The placeholder option is not a scientific segmentation baseline.

docs.title: 4.8.2 Why use the merged CHM?
docs.text:
For the complete BR01 survey, the merged product directory contains a single pit-free CHM and a complete normalized LAS. Running on the merged CHM avoids dividing the crown delineation into nine independent tile-level rasters and provides one continuous label domain. Tiled processing remains useful for large surveys; merging is preferable only when the complete raster is spatially coherent and fits the available resources. The installed FAST_ITD resolver returned merged_root, one CHM raster, and the expected pit-free variant for this dataset.

The BR01 merged inputs used in the verified experiment are:

ALS_tiles/Merged_ALS/
  ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m_FAST_CHM_pitfree.tif
  ALS-on_BR01_2019-07-05_300m_FAST_NORMALIZED.las

docs.title: 4.8.3 FAST_ITD deliverables
docs.text:
The observed complete-plot output was written under:

A shapefile is a multi-file dataset: retain its .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, and other associated files together. The current verified output is one combined crown shapefile containing many polygons, not one shapefile per crown. Per-tree crown shapefile export is a proposed enhancement and should not be documented as a published feature. Keep the combined layer as the canonical GIS deliverable, and maintain stable crown/tree IDs when any per-tree export is introduced.

docs.title: 4.9 FAST_TREECLOUDS: from crown labels to individual-tree LAS
docs.text:
FAST_TREECLOUDS uses the existing FAST_ITD crown segmentation and the complete normalized LAS. For BR01, the downstream run was performed from the same merged product root as the Yun2021 stage. This is a separate derivation; no reclassification, DEM, or CHM generation is requested.

docs.title: 4.9.1 LAS attributes and tree-cloud products
docs.text:
The BR01 combined segmented LAS exposes the following extra dimensions. These are identifiers and segmentation descriptors, not new physical measurements. Their exact relationships should be verified against the run's output manifest and the source label raster before interpreting tree counts.

LAS attribute Interpretation How readers should use it tree_id Assigned individual-tree identifier Group points for a tree; verify whether zero denotes unassigned points crown_id Crown-region identifier Relate point groups to crown polygons/labels crown_uid Crown identifier intended for cross-product reference Prefer for stable joins only after checking uniqueness parent_tree_id Parent tree association Inspect for hierarchical/merged tree associations segment_id Segmentation region or object identifier Trace subsegments where the implementation creates them obj_type Object/category code Decode from the installed writer before assigning semantic class names

A typical output root is Merged_ALS/FAST_TREECLOUDS/yun2021/chm/pitfree/FAST_NORMALIZED/. The workflow writes a combined LAS carrying segmentation attributes and, when --treeclouds_write_individual is enabled, an individual_trees/ directory. Each individual-tree LAS should preserve its source point coordinates, normalised heights, and supported point attributes. Verify the actual output manifest and individual file counts before publication.

docs.title: 4.9.2 Interpreting segmentation and validating tree clouds
docs.text: A successful extraction is not evidence that every crown corresponds to exactly one biological tree. Check crown/tree identifier consistency, duplicated IDs, canopy edge effects, point retention, and implausibly large or small individual-tree extents. The combined segmented LAS contains tree-related point attributes; the precise assignment behavior must be established from source and point records before drawing claims about understorey recovery or overlap handling. Visualize selected individual LAS clouds in 3D and compare them with the CHM-derived crown polygons.

docs.title: 4.9.3 Installation and release reproducibility
docs.text: The BR01 merged-root Yun2021 FAST_ITD command succeeded using the installed CLI. FAST_TREECLOUDS also succeeded for the merged-root workflow. Separately, the same local Conda installation was patched in fastgc/treeclouds.py to (i) search the sibling Merged_ALS directory when invoked from Processed_ALS, and (ii) copy LAS headers when exporting subsets. These are local installed-package changes, not confirmed changes to the published PyPI package or the development repository. Readers using an unpatched installation should use the tested Merged_ALS root and verify their installed version; the final book should be synchronized with a tested release before asserting portability.

docs.title: 4.9.4 Future software validation
docs.text: Exporting each crown as an individual shapefile, improving crown delineation with PyCrown-derived ideas, and ensuring matching tree IDs between polygon and LAS exports are development goals. PyCrown source integration requires a license and compatibility review; a controlled benchmark against the Yun2021 baseline is necessary before recommending an algorithm change. Preserve baseline outputs, run experiments in a separate namespace, and avoid treating geometric plausibility as reference-based accuracy.

docs.title: 4.10 Recovering products without reclassifying
docs.text:
A partially successful tile-run-merge job may leave classified tiles, DEM, and DSM already written. In that case, do not automatically rerun ground classification. Use derive-only on the existing Processed_ALS root after verifying required source folders. For the BR01 workspace used in the unsuccessful initial multi-target experiment, that root was:

G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\BR01_ALL_PRODUCTS_140m\ALS_tiles\Processed_ALS

  --in_path "G:\ALS_Jin\concurrent\BR01\ALS\BR01_ALL_PRODUCTS_140m\ALS_tiles\Processed_ALS" `
  --sensor_mode ALS `
  --workflow derive-only `
  --products FAST_NORMALIZED FAST_CHM `
  --grid_res 1.0 `
  --dem_method min `
  --jobs 8 `
  --chm_methods p2r p99 tin pitfree spikefree `
    percentile:pitfree:pct=5 `
    percentile_top:pitfree:low=5 `
    percentile_band:pitfree:low=2:high=8
Parameter Function Configuration guidance --in_path Existing processed product root Must contain FAST_GC and required upstream folders --workflow derive-only Reuse processed data Avoids ground classification rerun --products FAST_NORMALIZED FAST_CHM Derive missing products Existing DEM/DSM may be reused; inspect files before running --chm_methods Validated list of CHM targets Never include adaptive_pitfree in the current multi-method parser

Version caution: The installed derive-only source recognizes a Processed_ALS directory and checks for normalized data and DSM/DEM dependencies. Whether a particular output is skipped or overwritten depends on the installed version and its --skip_existing behavior. Back up results before experimentation.

docs.title: 4.11 Quality control and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause or interpretation Recommended check Input path not found Placeholder or wrong drive/file Test-Path -LiteralPath "..." before running CHM method rejected after earlier stages CLI/parser mismatch (adaptive_pitfree) Use the validated multi-target list; validate early Tile-edge seams Inadequate context or merge issue Inspect adjacent tile boundaries and core/buffer rules Missing DEM cells Sparse classified ground returns Inspect ground density and classification, not just interpolation CHM pits/spikes Sampling gaps or surface reconstruction Compare P2R, P99, pit-free, spike-free visually and against reference data Height-limited Fareed (2026) selector outputs Expected height-threshold point filtering Check pct, low, high against intended canopy stratum Excessive RAM/runtime Dense tiles or excessive workers Reduce concurrency or adjust tile dimensions Mixed multi-file outputs Incompatible source files or CRS Validate each survey before wall-to-wall merge

A successful command exit confirms execution, not accuracy. A book-quality validation should report ground/non-ground class counts, merged point preservation, seam checks, raster no-data coverage, CRS, and comparison to independent ground truth where available. Without such evidence, do not report accuracy metrics.

docs.title: 4.12 Reproducibility and next chapter
docs.text: The BR01 dataset and GeoTIFF products provide a repeatable illustration of ground classification → DEM → normalized points → DSM → alternative CHMs → Yun2021 ITD → FAST_TREECLOUDS. Site 5 supplies a separate performance comparison. The reader should retain the original LAS/LAZ, processing manifest, command, software version, hardware description, output file inventory, and elapsed time. The next chapter treats terrain derivatives and hydrological analysis as a separate analytical stage built upon the DEM.
